verdicts.reason: X judges whether a plan is stated up front; Y judges whether a stated plan would actually succeed -- a clearly-stated plan can still fail to reach the goal.
X is internal notational self-consistency; Y is fidelity to the question's own notation -- an answer can define its own symbols cleanly while still discarding the question's variables.
X targets whether a plan is announced before execution; Y targets whether a conclusion is stated at the end -- orthogonal points in the answer.

X is about matching vocabulary/explanation to the asker's general level; Y is about addressing the asker's specific attempt or confusion -- a reply can be pitched right yet ignore what the asker actually did.

X is honesty about the status of what was shown (not overclaiming); Y is completeness of delivering every component of a multi-part claim -- an answer can honestly flag a component as unfinished (X high, Y lower).
X wants the domain/range of mathematical claims stated; Y wants the range of applicability of a technique stated -- different objects (a claim's validity range vs a method's portability).
X is about staying on the exact problem posed; Y is specifically about flagging and repairing a defective/ambiguous question -- most well-posed questions make Y inapplicable while X still applies.
X checks the output is the right kind of deliverable (proof vs value vs reason); Y checks a proposed route actually reaches the goal -- type-match vs correctness-of-plan.
X is working the right problem; Y is delivering the right kind of output -- an answer can solve the exact asked problem yet deliver the wrong kind of thing (e.g. a value instead of a proof).
X is whether each step states its justification; Y is whether a final conclusion is stated at all -- justification-of-steps vs presence-of-conclusion.
X is naming the core difficulty of the problem; Y is whether a deliberate handover to the reader is actionable -- distinct objects (obstacle identification vs handover quality).
X wants ranges/domains stated for claims; Y wants the final assertion to be true and precisely stated -- stating scope vs being correct.

X is repairing/flagging a defective question; Y is whether a handed-over remainder is actionable -- an answer can fix an ambiguous question while completing all the work itself (Y inapplicable/different).
X is whether every part is load-bearing toward the conclusion (no decorative content); Y is whether the conclusion itself is explicitly stated -- relevance-of-parts vs explicitness-of-conclusion.
X is whether steps carry a stated justification; Y is whether the steps are mathematically correct -- a step can be justified yet wrong, or correct yet unjustified.
X is illustrating an abstraction with a worked concrete case; Y is whether every component of a multi-part claim is established -- pedagogical anchoring vs completeness.
X wants domains/ranges stated for claims; Y wants every component of a claim delivered -- scope-stating vs completeness, independent axes.
X is targeting the exact question asked; Y is whether a handover of remaining work is actionable -- an answer can solve the right problem and still leave an inactionable loose end, or vice versa.
X is stating a plan before execution; Y is each transition stating its licence -- an upfront plan can exist with unjustified steps later, or vice versa.

X is whether the decisive reason can be extracted as a standalone statement; Y is whether the argument is organized around one mechanism rather than a sprawl of attempts -- a single-mechanism proof can still never crystallize an explicit one-sentence 'why'.
X is whether a conclusion is explicitly stated; Y is whether that conclusion is mathematically true -- explicitness vs correctness, the paradigm case of two different objects.
X is relevance of every part to the conclusion; Y is whether cited external results are identifiable and given a role -- unrelated concerns.
X is working the exact problem asked; Y is using the question's own notation -- an answer can solve the right problem while still relabeling its variables.
X is notational hygiene (symbols defined, not reused); Y is correctness of intermediate mathematical statements -- clean notation does not imply correct steps.
X is whether hedging/doubt is localized to the specific uncertain step; Y is whether the answer engages the asker's specific attempt -- calibration-of-doubt vs responsiveness-to-asker.
X is stating a plan up front; Y is whether a handover of remaining work is actionable -- different stages/objects of the answer.
X targets correctness of the final assertion; Y targets correctness of the intermediate steps -- the canonical final-conclusion-vs-intermediate-steps split.
X is whether needed hypotheses are stated and shown to hold; Y is whether the final assertion is true and precise -- checking preconditions vs correctness of the endpoint.
X is motivating a specific non-obvious choice mid-argument; Y is whether the overall decisive reason for the result is extractable -- justifying a move vs crystallizing the result's central reason.
X wants domains/ranges stated for claims; Y wants an explicit conclusion -- scope-stating vs conclusion-presence.
X is whether a conclusion is stated; Y is whether a deliberate handover is actionable -- these largely apply to different kinds of answers (completed vs handed-off).
X is stating a plan before execution; Y is whether the decisive reason the result holds is extractable -- upfront framing vs after-the-fact explanatory payoff.
X is whether one mechanism organizes the whole argument; Y is whether edge/boundary cases are handled or excluded -- structural unity vs case coverage.
X is motivating why a non-obvious choice was made; Y is each transition stating what licenses its validity -- strategic justification of a move vs formal justification of a step's correctness.

X is not trivializing a load-bearing step with dismissive language; Y is every part being relevant to the conclusion -- an answer can be entirely on-topic (no decorative content) while still waving through its crux step with 'clearly'.

X is illustrating an abstract claim with a worked example for intuition; Y is verifying a produced result (substitution/special case check) -- pedagogical anchoring vs correctness verification, dissociable purposes.
X is naming an applied method and its general range of applicability; Y is naming external cited sources and their specific role here -- portability-of-technique vs locatability-of-citation.
X is working the exact problem asked; Y is whether a proposed route actually reaches the goal -- correct target vs correct plan.
X is accuracy of claimed status (not overclaiming); Y is whether needed hypotheses are stated and verified to hold -- self-report honesty vs precondition-checking.
X is whether a conclusion is stated; Y is whether a proposed route reaches the goal -- explicitness of endpoint vs validity of a proposed plan.

X is announcing a plan/goal before execution; Y is motivating specific non-obvious choices as they arise -- an upfront plan can be stated without individual tactical choices being justified, and vice versa.

X penalizes dismissive trivializing language on load-bearing steps; Y grades how specifically an omission is named for reconstruction -- a non-dismissive but vague pointer scores fine on X yet poorly on Y, and a dismissive-but-specifically-named skip can diverge the other way.
X is whether the weight of tools/machinery fits the problem; Y is whether the answer targets the exact question asked -- proportionality of method vs correctness of problem selection.
X is symbol definition/consistency; Y is domains/ranges stated for claims -- both are rigor criteria but over different objects (symbols vs validity ranges).
X is targeting the exact problem asked; Y is whether a conclusion is explicitly stated -- an answer can work the right problem and still trail off without stating its conclusion.
X is motivating a specific non-obvious choice; Y is naming the overall obstacle the problem poses -- justifying a move vs diagnosing the problem's core difficulty.

X is accuracy of claimed status (not overclaiming); Y is whether hedging is localized to the specific uncertain step rather than diffuse -- an answer can avoid overclaiming while still hedging vaguely across everything.
X is relevance of every part to the conclusion; Y is whether one single mechanism organizes the whole argument -- an answer can have two relevant-but-unintegrated approaches (X high, Y lower).
X is whether the output is the requested kind of thing (value/proof/reason); Y is whether a conclusion is explicitly stated -- type-match vs explicitness of the ending statement.
Both are verbatim paraphrases asking whether the final stated answer/conclusion is mathematically correct.
Both are verbatim paraphrases asking whether symbols are defined before their first use.
Naming the key obstacle is a substantive judgement about the argument; amount of displayed LaTeX is a superficial formatting count -- unrelated concepts.
Verifying hypotheses hold is a substantive rigor judgement; word count is a superficial length metric -- unrelated concepts.
